speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The reason for budget secrecy, I submit, and this is borne out by the precedents both here and in Westminster, is that knowledge of fiscal and monetary proposals before they are announced in the budget by the minister could enable those who have access to the knowledge to profit therefrom. The Leader of the Opposition referred to budget secrecy in a rather different context, and I find myself wholly in agreement with him, that there ought to be the most open possible discussion of economic policy, but budget secrecy relates only to questions relating to the fisc, as my friend the Minister of Finance said after his budget speech.
For example, advance knowledge of a change in the sales or excise tax or customs duties could enable someone to purchase or import goods before the change came into effect, thus cheating the revenue as well as profiting himself or herself. Similarly, advance knowledge of a change in the corporate tax could enable the insider to speculate profitably on the stock market. It is possible too that advance knowledge of the general fiscal and monetary policy of the government as enunciated in the budget could be turned to advantage on the stock or bond markets, or even in the foreign exchange market.
The tradition of budget secrecy, therefore, as my colleague the Minister of Finance said in the House when a question arose about the announcement of changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act, relates to the fisc, and does not necessarily relate to other matters of government policy which the government may see fit to authorize the Minister of Finance to announce or refer to in his budget address.
Hon. members will recall that in this particular case of the proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act there is no way by which advance knowledge could profit anyone who knew in advance what was to happen. As the minister himself pointed out, there has been a great deal of public discussion, pro and con, in recent years about the desirability of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act, and the government made no secret whatever of the fact that it had been consulting its own supporters in this House on the subject.

The Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, other members of the cabinet, and certain officials do have knowledge of the contents of the budget before it is delivered in the House. This is unavoidable. The tradition of budget secrecy applies to them in a peculiar way. Not only are they bound not to reveal the contents of the budget before it is delivered, they are bound to act in their private affairs as if they were not aware of its contents.
This is probably the principal reason why Ministers of Finance, past and present, do not burden their colleagues with knowledge of their intentions with respect to tax changes very far in advance of budget day.
When I was Minister of Finance I consulted with the Prime Minister a couple of weeks in advance on proposed major tax changes, gave a broad indication of the alternatives to my colleagues a week in advance, and then in as short a time as I could just before budget day I told them what my final proposals would be. My successors in office have followed very much the same pattern.
Needless to say it is not an ideal sort of consultation, but it seems unavoidable if the Minister of Finance is to save his colleagues from the burden of knowing for some time before the budget what tax changes will come into effect on that day. Most of them, I am confident, would prefer not to know much in advance, so that they do not have to fear that their behaviour would be subject to misinterpretation or misrepresentation. When the Minister of Finance raised questions in his speech about the applicability of the tradition of secrecy to modern budgets, I had a fellow feeling arising from my own experience.
For example, what about changes in the rates of personal income tax, one of the most important sources of revenue and one of the most important instruments for effecting individual spending and saving, and the distribution of revenues between the provinces and the federal government? Does it matter whether the government's intentions with respect to changes in the personal income tax are known in advance of the budget presentation? I doubt it very much. There is no way I can think of whereby advance information on the subject could enable a taxpayer to profit or to cheat the revenue. One comes to the conclusion that the tradition of budget secrecy, which originated when governments raised their revenues primarily from customs and excise taxes, has been extended in a rather meaningless way to the personal income tax, to which it has little if any relevance.
There is a strong case for limiting the tradition of budget secrecy to the areas in which it has relevance, and to permit the Minister of Finance a great deal more latitude in discussing personal income tax changes and matters of a similar kind which do not have market or speculative significance.
The minister should be free, moreover, I suggest, to discuss changes in the structure of taxation without being found guilty of breach of budget secrecy. What should be secret is the government's final decision on tax changes where advance information could be profitable to the insider. This does not mean necessarily that the Minister of Finance would have an obligation to anticipate his budget proposals in any field. He should not be in the
June 8, 1976

position, however, where he cannot discuss changes of the kinds I have mentioned outside the closed circle of his departmental advisers and cabinet in preparation of his budget proposals for fear of offending the principle of budgetary secrecy.
I have only one suggestion to offer, which is that the best defence the Minister of Finance could make would be to make it abundantly clear that he was having such consultations, and to have them as open as possible so that everyone knows the consultations are taking place.
I should now like to turn to the question of implementation of the fiscal proposals of the budget. This procedure, the business of ways and means, is a most complicated matter for it is not only part of the foundation of parliament but also it is of immense importance to everyone in the country. In a parliamentary system the government must take full responsibility for fiscal matters; if parliament cannot be induced to accept the government's proposals on taxation, the life of the government must come to an end. Since taxation policy is so fundamental to the retention of office, we have developed the rule concerning the financial initiative of the Crown, that is, a rule preventing any member of parliament, except a minister, from initiating a measure to impose a tax, to increase the rate of an existing tax, or to extend the incidence of an existing tax.
The second principle governing taxation matters in parliament is that fiscal measures must be introduced in the first instance in the House of Commons. We have never even conceded to the Senate the right to amend such proposals.
If we look at the United States we see quite a different procedure. While the President of the United States may communicate his proposals on tax policy to the Congress, they are put into a tangible form not by the administration but by a committee of the House of Representatives. Tax bills usually undergo many metamorphoses on their way through Congress-the United States Senate can and often does amend such measures-and when ready for the President's signature, very likely are quite different from his original proposals.
Taxation measures in the Unites States, however, are not normally retroactive; they come into effect on a given date which occurs sometime after a tax bill becomes law. This is also true of some of our provinces, such as Ontario. In our parliament, however, we have adopted the British practice of making most tax proposals effective virtually immediately they are announced. This requires, of course, some sort of formal notice to persons or corporations whose taxes are changed so quickly. For this reason we have arrived at our procedure concerning Notices of Ways and Means.
A Notice of Ways and Means has two effects. First, as I said, it provides notice of tax changes to those affected. In this function it should be in as much detail as possible. Its second effect, however, is to protect the financial initiative of the Crown.
Only a minister may table a Notice of Ways and Means, and a motion to concur in it cannot be debated or amended. Tax bills, however, must be based on one or more Notices of Ways and Means, and since their pith and substance
The Budget-Mr. Sharp
must be the same as that of the Notices of Ways and Means they become most difficult to amend. Before 1969 the Notices of Ways and Means were considered in a committee of the whole, as many members now in the House will recall, and could, within the limits of the financial initiative of the Crown, be amended. In other words, if the government could be persuaded to make changes, our procedures lent themselves to amendments. The tax bills that followed the ways and means resolutions became, except in the case of the most controversial proposals, exercises in detail for the House.
Under our present procedures, however, the government itself cannot even propose amendments to a tax bill that would increase the rates or extend the incidence of the proposed tax. Since the Notices of Ways and Means, in order to provide as much information as possible, tend to be so explicit that they appear almost as bills, the scope for amendments to bills based on them is even more restricted.
Our difficulty is that if we provide maximum information to the taxpayers at the earliest possible time by making the Notices of Ways and Means explicit, we also thereby limit most severely the scope for amendments to the bill. If, on the other hand, we make the Notices of Ways and Means more general in order to expand the scope for amendments, since the bills based thereon cannot be introduced until the budget debate is completed, for several weeks the taxpayers may be denied the detailed information they require in order to make their plans.
I do not suggest, however, that we revert to the old committee of ways and means procedure. That merely imposed a redundant stage to the fiscal procedure. Debate tended to repeat the formal budget debate and to anticipate debate on the bill. My suggestion is that we endeavour to find a procedure whereby from time to time a sort of Supplementary Notice of Ways and Means could be brought down in order to permit specified amendments. We have, in fact, done this on occasion, but only with unanimous consent. Perhaps now we should provide for such a practice in our rules.
One other part of our ways and means procedure that we ought to consider is the rule that requires all tax measures to be referred, after second reading, to a committee of the whole. This one is perhaps a more doubtful proposal, but one which I think should be examined again. The theory behind this rule is that taxation is of such general interest and importance that every member should be on the committee considering the bill. Experience, however, does not square with this theory. While committees of the whole on tax bills are reasonably well attended because of possible votes, most of the speeches seem to be made for reading by constituents and should really be made in the budget debate or at third reading.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not really criminal.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. I am just being factual. Only a handful of members on either side of the House really participate in the process of explaining and refining the bill. One cannot help but wonder whether tax bills, or at least most of them, ought not to be referred to a standing committee.

The Budget-Mr. Sharp
This brings me to the procedures which have evolved in recent years relating to the handling of the budget speech in the House and outside. These procedures evolved essentially to ensure the necessary secrecy while at the same time enabling the various media to give adequate and speedy coverage to the contents of the budget.
I have not been able to consult the records but I have been told that the special procedures for media coverage of the budget began either during the Second World War or shortly thereafter. As I recall it, at the beginning, at the time when as a civil servant I was concerned with these matters, the special procedure consisted of giving the media the first part of the speech which did not contain any tax changes when the minister rose to speak, and the remainder when the minister reached that point in his speech. This gave the press an opportunity of putting the story on the wires of the print media somewhat more quickly than if it had had to report the minister as he spoke. Radio stations were able to broadcast the tax changes more or less simultaneously with the minister's speech.
The next development was the locked room, which was aimed at giving the media an opportunity of doing a more thorough job of analyzing the budget proposals while preserving the necessary secrecy. It meant, of course, that those privileged to be locked up were in a position to wire and broadcast the contents of the budget just as soon as the doors were opened and even before the minister had uttered a word of his speech in the House of Commons.
To me, the resulting situation is deplorable and has made a mockery of this House and its membership. What made it even more disturbing, I regret to say, is that the minister himself appeared this year on television screens on a pretaped interview, recorded during the lock-up, talking about a budget he had not even finished delivering, and his critics who had also been in the lock-up appeared on the same screen replying to a speech they had not yet heard.
I understand how this deplorable situation evolved and I am not being critical of either the minister or the other MPs. One thing led to another, each logical and defensible in itself to meet a particular problem. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come to put an end to a procedure which I believe is an affront to this House.
What is the problem? It is that the people of Canada do not have an opportunity of seeing and listening to the Minister of Finance delivering his speech. If they could do so, a substantial change in the procedure now being followed to meet the requirements of the media, print or electronic, would be possible and would eliminate most of the odious results.
Fortunately it is now possible for everyone in Canada who is interested to be able to watch and listen to the budget speech and the replies of the opposition. All we have to do is to broadcast our proceedings by radio and television, just as my colleague and his critics broadcast their commentary outside the House while the minister was speaking here in the House, making us all very uncomfortable.
It will be astounding, Mr. Speaker, if we members of parliament will ever again be content to sit listening to the

Minister of Finance read his speech, waiting for him to reach the point where he announces the proposed tax changes while the reporters on radio and TV, with the document in their hands, talk confidently about what the minister will say before he concludes. It is an affront, and I trust that come next budget there will be a demand from all sides of the House that this farce will not be permitted to recur.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When our proceedings are broadcast-and I say when rather than if, because I see no alternative to the present procedures for lock-up and advance knowledge, except broadcast-I am sure that the minister will also want to deliver his message in a form more suitable to the electronic media-a shorter speech which he can supplement by a written document to be appended to Hansard- and that the opposition critics will want to make their comments the same evening so that they can be broadcast directly from the House. Not only will this be good for the broadcast, it will also make the House a more lively place on budget night.
The timing of the budget speech should also be reviewed when our proceedings are broadcast. It is accepted that the contents of the budget should not be revealed until the markets are closed. That is why the budget speech is delivered in the evening rather than in the afternoon. An eight o'clock starting time is rather late, however, for the print media if the morning papers of the following day are to carry a full account of the budget. While it would be unusual for the House to sit say between five and seven o'clock, or between six and eight on budget day, some such special arrangement should be considered. This kind of arrangement would also afford the electronic media plenty of opportunity to fill the rest of the evening with commentary from observers across the country who would already have watched and listened to the budget speech being delivered.
In the interests of adequate coverage there could continue to be a lock-up, the doors being opened for the reporters when the Minister of Finance had concluded his speech which, if my suggestions were adopted, would be either at seven or eight o'clock. It would also be suitable, I suggest, to include in the lock-up the spokesmen for the opposition who would be expected to follow the minister in the House debate. They are included now, they could be included in the kind of changed circumstances that I have outlined. These MPs could be released from the locked rooms when the minister rose to deliver his speech so that they could hear it, on the understanding that they would not bring a copy of the speech into the House or reveal its contents to anyone in advance of the delivery of the minister's speech.
There is on the order paper a resolution seeking approval of the broadcasting of our proceedings. Because of the press of other business it is not the intention of the government to call that resolution for debate before the adjournment. I have today, however, tabled a document giving an estimate of the costs of installing broadcast equipment and of annual operating costs so that there can be some further public discussion of the proposal.
The arguments I have put forward for broadcasting the budget apply with equal force to the whole of our proceed-
June 8, 1976

ings. The people of Canada should see parliament in action, and not have to be content to read about it or watch others talking about it. If we believe in parliament, as all of us do, then we should be proud to have it broadcast. A limited number of Canadians-very limited today-are privileged to watch from the galleries. It is now open to us to have the whole of the population observe our proceedings. When that happens then the various media can fulfil more effectively their respective functions. They will still be privileged to interview MP's in room 130-S or elsewhere. They can still comment. But the interviews and the commentary will no longer be a substitute for parliamentary democracy in action on the floor of this House.
It is my hope that early in the new session we will take the decision to broadcast our proceedings and bring parliament to the people. We should cease the farce of the kind of proceedings we had this year on the budget, which are completely unnecessary and an affront to the House. I hope everyone in the House will see that it never happens again.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to preface my remarks in the budget debate by coming down from the huge statistics that we heard this afternoon from other speakers, statistics which relate to the country as a whole, and begin my brief address by simply referring to the city where I live. I think this somehow sets the tone for the entire budget, at least from the point of view of those of us who sit on this side of the House.
I have here a clipping from the June 5 edition of the Brantford Expositor which states that the number of jobless continues to rise in Brant county. In Brant county the present unemployment figure was 4,954 persons in May, chasing approximately 200 job vacancies. Yet there are people in my constituency who say that those on unemployment insurance are lazy, that they will not get out and hustle for a job. We are talking in terms of 9 per cent unemployment, or almost 5,000 unemployed registered at Manpower chasing 200 jobs in an industrial city which has many small industries and three or four large industries. I think this is indicative of many parts of the country because if it is that bad in Brantford, which is in southern Ontario, I wonder just how bad it is elsewhere. Of course we know how bad it is in places like Cape Breton Island, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, northern Ontario, parts of Quebec and parts of the west and northwest.
Much of the press reported that the finance minister faced a dilemma in trying to bring down a budget which would tackle the dual problems of high inflation and high unemployment. A few days after the budget speech it was generally conceded by many that the minister had done little or nothing to solve either of these critical problems. In fact his budget will make them worse.
There were no provisions in the budget which will do anything about our disastrous unemployment rate, nor were there any measures introduced which will increase productivity and, generally speaking, put our economy back on the road to recovery. For these omissions criticism is demanded from all members on this side of the House, or
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
from as many as possible who can speak during these few short days in the debate.
Criticism is also warranted for the fact that even if the goal of less than 9 per cent inflation is attained next year, inflation will remain unacceptably high in this country. The finance minister patted himself and the government on the back with a statement on page 11 of the budget speech which reads, and I quote, "the actual rate of inflation has slowed noticeably since the introduction" of the prices and incomes program. He went on, "This sharp reduction in the rate of price increase is very welcome." What this overlooks is that the drop in the rate of increase in the consumer price index is occurring in areas not controlled by the Anti-Inflation Board. For instance, food costs declined at an annual rate of 5 per cent to 6 per cent, but are expected to rise considerably in the next few months, particularly this autumn.
The recent increase in the price of oil and petroleum products will also seriously affect the rate of inflation, and prices will continue to increase.
In the areas of inflation and unemployment I would certainly agree that this was a do nothing budget. What is deplorable, however, is the fact that action was sorely needed on both these fronts and, as one newspaper columnist pointed out, the minister, and I quote, "administered a placebo budget, hoping to keep the patient"-that is, the economy-"quiet until things get better by themselves." Things will not get better by themselves.
I have mentioned the fact that the Anti-Inflation Board, by and large, is useless in trying to control rising prices. In this connection I was interested in the public relations campaign the board has launched which outlines the kinds of increases it cannot control. Among some of the items the Anti-Inflation Board claims it is not responsible for are tobacco, alcohol, hydro, gas, water rates, public transit rates, rents, medical insurance premiums, and heating oil. In other words the inflationary pressures will not be halted on goods and services which are a daily necessity, not a luxury, to all Canadians.
On the unemployment side we find that in April of this year Canada showed the highest unemployment rate since June of 1961, and there are strong indications that it is unlikely to decline during the rest of this year. The minister's own Economic Review in April had this to say:
During the recession firms engaged in substantial labour hoarding. The number of persons employed did not decline in line with cutbacks in output. Average hours were reduced . . . Much greater use was made of part time employment. Thus during the initial period of recovery firms can obtain increases in output without any increases in the number of workers by simply using them more intensively, while underutilized plant and equipment are pushed towards better operating rates.
In view of this it was absolutely crucial for the minister to have addressed himself more closely to the unemployment problem. At one point, on page 19 of his speech, the minister offered hope that some employment programs would be offered. Instead, all we got was a statement to the effect that direct employment programs can have broad social value and are not simply make work, but no proposals were made. The government even did away with OFY this year despite many thousands of unemployed young people coming on to the labour market.

June 8, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
I gather that the government is resigned to going through the rest of this year with unemployment at about 7 per cent of the labour force, hoping that the 7.4 per cent rate recorded in April was a fluke and not a real upturn. The finance minister's economic plan, if we can call it that, is based on the fact that the Canadian economy will generate more than 250,000 new jobs this year. This sounds impressive until we take into account that the labour force has been growing at well over 300,000 per year for the last three years. If the 250,000 jobs the minister talks about are added to the present employment level, we shall still be left with 747,000 people out of work by the end of this year. That is not what I call real performance.
The minister vainly tried to soften the impact of the current unemployment level by citing the study on the unemployed of the Economic Council of Canada, which said that much of today's jobless figure is accounted for by the young, by housewives, and by people dissatisfied with their former jobs seeking contentment in other kinds of work. I ask, why should this make any difference? Should a housewife feel any less discontented at being unable to secure work because her husband is currently drawing a salary? Should a young person feel any less distressed after having completed training for a particular job and being unable to find one, just because the finance minister says hers or his is not a kind of unemployment? I suggest that no government should be so complacent that it can afford not to provide jobs for those who wish to work, and by far the greater majority in this country want to work.
Therefore on two major fronts, inflation and unemployment, nothing has been done. As I mentioned, as a result of the omissions, both may be exacerbated.
Turning now to the specific measures which were introduced, it seems to me that it was totally inappropriate to cut $300 million in insurance benefits from the unemployed. On the one hand the minister says that today's unemployment does not carry with it the hardships it once did because of programs such as unemployment insurance, while on the other hand he announced that eligibility for benefits would be substantially cut back. It is a good thing we have some of these social transfer payments because I suggest that if we did not we would be in the grip of a revolution in this country today, for Canadians will not accept breadlines or soup kitchens any more. As a result of the cutback, some 330,000 individuals will not be eligible for unemployment insurance.
The manpower minister in his speech to the House on June 2 tried to dispel this figure with convoluted logic. He said that the figure of 330,000 did not mean that at any moment of time in the year 330,000 people would be affected. He said, and I quote, "Because the average duration of benefits extends only for a portion of the year, at any moment in time, only about 100,000 individuals would be affected." Before pursuing this argument further I must say that I find it absolutely appalling that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) would use the phrase "only about 100,000". That is 100,000 Canadians- 100,000 individuals who live in this country. Nevertheless he continued this line of thought, and said that of this 100,000, 50 per cent will be able to find instant work for an additional four weeks. This means, and again I quote from the minister's speech, "only about 50,000 individuals would

not be able to receive benefits and of these 80 per cent have no dependants". He has got it down to almost zero if you follow his line of thinking.
[DOT] <1740)
The minister, like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), has introduced the idea of degrees of seriouness for the unemployed. If you are single and unemployed, the government is of the opinion that your problem is not all that serious. Only this government, Mr. Speaker, could show such callousness. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration's manipulation of figures prompted one journalist to quip, "Mr. Andras leaves us wondering why we need an unemployment insurance scheme at all, until we realize that his entire rationale is a piece of statistical hocus pocus."
The proposed changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act are simply others in a line of changes introduced by this government which show how incompetent and impotent the administration is in dealing with unemployment. The last changes in Bill C-69 were a clear admission by the Liberals that they could not bring the jobless rate down, and consequently they were not about to pay for their inadequacies either.
The new proposals which were introduced will have disastrous effects on marginal workers, particularly those in Atlantic Canada, the northern part of Ontario, parts of Quebec, and parts of the northwest. There are thousands of people in this country who are employed in occupations where they cannot have a job that lasts for more than eight weeks. By raising the eligibility requirements from 8 to 12 weeks the government is essentially saying to these marginal workers that it is their fault that they cannot find lasting jobs. I suggest it is the government's fault for not providing jobs for them.
Why was such a move contemplated, Mr. Speaker? The leader of my party suggested last Wednesday that part of the justification for the changes rests with some of the myths that are held about unemployment insurance and the unemployed. The member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) cited the notion held by many in this country that there are plenty of jobs available for all those who want them. Yet, as has been stated, there are more than 12 men and women available for every one job across the country. I relate this to my own constituency, Brant county. If all the jobs were taken that are available, there would still be 700,000 people in this country out of work. Those are the facts; surely the government knows that also, but instead it reacted to the myth with a totally irrational proposal.
There are other myths about unemployment insurance and the unemployed. Some believe that benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Commission Act are too generous and that this leads to a disincentive to work. Yet we know that last year the average weekly benefit paid was $84.64. How many family bills, how many mortgage payments can be made on that amount of money? The very study that some have used to show that the UIC Act provides a disincentive to work, done by the Economic Council of Canada, also said that most surveys show that the vast majority of Canadians prefer work, not unemployment insurance.
June 8, 1976

Probably the most outstanding comment made in the Economic Council of Canada report on the unemployment insurance system was the following: "Notwithstanding how the effects of the 1971 changes-have been interpreted, one point is unquestionably clear: regulatory changes alone do not, will not, send people back to work, if there are no jobs available." This is what the New Democratic Party has been saying for quite some time.
The costs o! unemployment insurance in Canada could be brought down if the government could manage the economy of this country in such a fashion that jobs would be provided to all those who wanted them. I said at the outset that the Minister of Finance had absolutely no intention of dealing with unemployment. Instead of dealing with the problem itself, the minister decided to take a crack at those who are unemployed.
In this regard I would like to make passing mention of the comments made by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) last Wednesday. In his concluding remarks he said, as reported at page 14097 of Hansard, "The NDP want people to rely on unemployment just as the government does, and this-we object to most strenuously." The member for Hamilton West made this statement, or used it as the main reason why our party's amendment was unacceptable to the members to my right. I should clarify for the hon. member that the NDP has never wanted people to rely on unemployment. As a matter of fact our party, the socialist party, is a work oriented party, not a party oriented to living off the avails of someone else just because of laziness.
We want to put people to work. If you look at other countries in the world that have social democratic parties in power you will find in most cases that unemployment is very low. However, we are adamantly opposed to any measures which would restrict the eligibility of any person who is out of work for some reason totally beyond his or her control. Let me reiterate that the only acceptable way of reducing the cost of unemployment insurance in this country is to provide the required jobs. In other words, put people to work.
We in this party feel that certain steps could have been taken to alleviate some of the unemployment facing Canada. The Canadian economy is presently functioning at approximately 80 per cent capacity. What this means is that there is room for expansion in our economy. Tax cuts could have been provided without fuelling inflation. An increased demand for goods would have stimulated the economy, and consequently manufacturing industries would call back men and women who needed the jobs. As I said, Mr. Speaker, this stimulation for the economy would not have caused further inflation; it would if we were operating at full capacity, but this is not the present case.
Let me address myself briefly to some of the other budgetary measures introduced on May 25. I wish to deal specifically with two matters-the increase in deductions for child care expenses from the old maximum of $2,000 per family to a total annual limit of $4,000, and increasing to $3,500 the maximum annual amount deductible by employees and employers in respect of a registered pension plan. Also, if an individual is not a member of a pension plan, the maximum contribution limit will be increased from the present $4,000 to $5,500.
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
I should like to emphasize that I am not personally opposed to people being able to increase their tax deductions if they are able to save. If they have money that they can save without paying further tax, through registered retirement savings or the registered home owners' savings plan which is being made more flexible, I am not critical of them. If they earn around $18,000 or $20,000 a year and wish to set aside tax deferred savings until they are older, that is fine. But what I most strenuously object to is the fact that this is considered to be a very liberal attitude in a budgetary form for the people of Canada. We are talking about a very, very small number of Canadians. They are the only people who get a break at all in this budget because the vast majority of people in this country have no chance of saving $3,500 or $4,000 every year, or even $5,500 for a retirement savings plan.
Why did the Minister of Finance not bring in tax cuts for low income people to balance things and make it a much more equitable budget? These tax changes have been referred to as a hidden welfare system by Reuben Baetz of the Canadian Council on Social Development. Actually the government's tax deferral schemes are exactly that. Mr. Baetz was referring to such measures as well as to measures introduced in the last several budgets, one example being the $1,000 interest income deductible from income for income tax purposes. Such measures help people in higher income brackets. One must seriously question whether spending $60 million-which is what the deductions actually cost us-to aid those with incomes of $20,000 a year and more, really met one of Canada's socially pressing needs. I am convinced that the measure did not fill a pressing need felt by most Canadians.
With respect to deductions made in connection with registered retirement savings plans, I suggest that in order to reach the former ceiling of $4,000 a taxpayer had to earn $20,000 a year. The new ceiling of $5,500 per year means a further tax saving of almost $700 for a single person earning $27,500, but not a penny of saving for the average Canadian. We had become used to seeing the former minister of finance redistribute income in this fashion. I hoped the present minister would change the pattern. Unfortunately he did not.
The measure to increase deductions for child care expenses has been lauded by many; again, would it not have been more equitable if the $15 million, the estimated cost of this measure, had been given as a flat rate credit? Since deductions provide higher benefits to those in top income brackets, the child care deductions will obviously benefit those who need them least.
The government's record of income distribution is abysmal. For instance the share of total income going to the bottom 20 per cent of income earners was less in 1974 than in 1951. Not only has income distribution not changed substantially in the last quarter century, but successive ministers of finance, the present minister included, have introduced measures like those I referred to which have made the income tax system much less progressive.
I do not know how much longer we must wait for an equitable tax system. I suggest to the Minister of Finance, the cabinet and colleagues on my right, that unless we put

June 8, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Balfour
people back to work in meaningful jobs with security of tenure, correct the inequities in our tax system, improve the lot of the 20 per cent to 25 per cent of our population living in abject poverty, give young people more incentive to study and qualify for meaningful jobs, correct the deplorable situation in which thousands of our qualified nurses who could not find work in this country went to the United States for work, and give incentives for young, middle aged, and older Canadians to look for meaningful work, this country will be in great trouble in two or three years.
We saw what happened the other day on Parliament Hill. The violent behaviour of the few troublemakers in the large crowd disgusted us. I suggest that if the Anti-Inflation Board continues to be unfair we shall see more violent demonstrations. There will be more violence in this country. There will be an even greater division between those who possess some wealth and those who possess none. The members of this House are obliged to make sure this does not happen. What other assembly in the country, what other elected council has power to make the vital decisions which will bring about more economic and social equity in this country?
