subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I address my remarks tonight to the failure of the May 25 budget to deal significantly with the problems facing industry in this country. A columnist for the Montreal Gazette in commenting on the government's new budget, or non-budget as it should be called, described the government's effort most accurately when he said, and I quote:
Economy, heal thyself: having studied the symptoms for nine months, Canada's new fiscal physician has decided he does not know what to do, anymore than John Turner did when the chills of high unemployment came at the same time as the fever of inflation.
So he has administered a placebo budget, hoping to keep the patient quiet until things get better by themselves. Perhaps the Yankee medicine of export demand from the United States will help.
Perhaps the private sector-written off by the Prime Minister only a few months ago-will deliver the right goods and services to the right place at the right time and the right price. We had better hope so.
The Minister of Finance can expect criticism for bringing down, in the midst of multiplied economic problems, the kind of drifting, dreamy budget which might have been produced by a Finance Minister afraid to change anything because things were going so well.
But things are not going all that well, Mr. Speaker. The minister will live with a deficit of about $4.5 billion for

another year, an amount which points to the government's failure to control its own spending.
Furthermore, the budget does little or nothing to fight unemployment, increase productivity, restrain growth of government spending, reduce Canada's high interest and exchange rates, or promote business investment. In short, the budget exemplifies the government's obvious ineptitude in coming to grips with our real problems and needs.
The budget makes no significant effort to tackle the four major problem areas facing the Canadian economy inflation, unemployment, productivity, and the current account deficit.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce has termed this do-nothing budget "a very anti-business budget", and so it is. The industrial and business sector of this country does not need government apathy. Rather, business and industry in Canada need the incentives that government can provide to improve plant efficiency, re-equip, improve the supply of goods and services, and compete effectively on the international market.
One area where the government could have helped improve the well-being of Canadian industry is the field of research and development. On March 12 of this year the Council of the Academy of Science of the Royal Society of Canada made it clear to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that a serious situation exists, and promises to become more serious in the future, as a result of the government's non-policy for the support of scientific research and development. The society, in its brief to the Prime Minister, said:
At no time in our history have we been confronted with so many problems needing science-based solutions. It is hardly possible to exaggerate the importance of the decisions that confront Canada in such areas as resource management, energy options, health care, food supply, pollution, transportation, and so on.
Furthermore, the choices that we, as a nation, make in these areas will be dependent on the maturity, knowledge, versatility and statute of contemporary Canadian science and engineering. Canada cannot afford to depend on the scientific and engineering skills of other countries to solve its problems.
Even choices as to the best kinds of technology to be imported and adapted to Canadian conditions . . . must be made on the basis of sound scientific and engineering knowledge, which can only be obtained from a community of highly competent and active Canadian scientists and engineers.
Having said that, the Council of the Academy expressed a great concern with the unfortunate deterioration that the government has allowed to take place, a dangerous deterioration in the public support of research and development in Canadian industry, in government laboratories and in universities.
The government has a bad habit of ignoring the sound advice of those sectors of society which specialize in a given field of endeavour, and it therefore comes as no surprise that the government has made a failure of its limited efforts in this area. Although the need for a well funded Canadian industrial research effort is recognized by most, the government has, as usual, headed in the opposite and wrong direction.
A statement on science policy put out by the offices of Bell Canada illustrates this point. I quote:
We refer to the government decision to freeze research expenditures, to repeal the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act
June 8, 1976

(IRDIA) and to reduce the money available for the Program for the Advancement of Industrial Technology (PAIT).
While the sums involved are not great (we are led to believe that the annual grants through IRDIA do not exceed $30 million) they were often essential for the initiation and continuation of the research programs of some companies.
Money allotted to research and development at the best of times could only be described as minuscule. The fact of the matter is that Canada's expenditures on research and development peaked in 1966, and Canada has never spent more than 1.2 per cent of its Gross National Product on research. Other industrialized nations such as Japan, West Germany, France, the United States, and Britain, have all committed much larger amounts of GNP to research and continue to do so. It must be said that if this nation expects to expand industrially, to become a major international trading nation and to continue the improvements in its internal social well-being, then this country cannot afford not to have research. The fact of the matter is that Canada will be outpaced by other industrial countries and will end up purchasing technology and scientific expertise from elsewhere.
As one who takes more than a passing interest in the economic climate of this country 1 recognize, unlike the government, that there is a real economic value attached to increased efficiency, better products, and increased trade. If that sounds like a cold view of the matter, then just remember that better medical care, improved housing, superior consumer goods, less work, and increased prosperity are also attributable to scientific and technological advancement. It would seem that the government views research and development expenditures as a luxury which can be done without. This is one area, however, where continued and increased government support is required. Research and development is not an expense; it is an investment in the future of this country.
Canada has problems quite peculiar to its own development. There is little to contest the precept that Canada's economic future largely depends upon its ability to enlarge its position as an international trader. Industrial research can undoubtedly be one key to securing and advancing a position in international trade for this country. Certain facts of Canadian economic life must not be forgotten when we discuss this subject.
Over the past few years wage levels in this country have risen at a rate much faster than those of competing nations and nations to which Canada hopes to sell. Unfortunately at the same time the level of productivity in Canada has dropped in relation to that of such countries as West Germany and the United States. And so it is that we are handicapped from the word go in trying to compete in many foreign markets.
To compensate for the higher wage levels and decreased productivity in Canada, research and development can bring innovations to products and manufacturing practices. To ignore research and development at this time can only lead to further deficits in the Canadian balance of trade in the future, as Canada fails to make inroads into foreign markets. It must be stressed again and again to the government that Canada's trade position is unhealthy. Canada in reality had a current trade deficit of $8 billion
The Budget-Mr. Balfour
in 1975. We covered it by selling a net of $2.9 billion in raw resources, borrowing $4.7 billion from foreign sources, and letting our exchange reserves fall by $400 million. With a current account deficit of $5.1 billion in 1975, even after the trade surplus of $2.9 billion in raw materials, it is difficult to conceive of our trade deficit being any more ominous.
Quite apart from the likelihood of our 1976 trade performance being little better than in 1975, however, the composition of the 1975 current account balance is a source of even greater alarm than the deficit figures would indicate. The sale of raw materials is, of course, a basic element in the economic picture of this country. Increased sales of raw materials may be one way out of our current trade problems. However, most of us, except the government, realize that this attitude is pure folly. Exporting crude materials provides considerably less benefit to the Canadian economy than exporting fully or partly manufactured goods. There is far more value added to a manufactured product, in terms of labour, capital investment, and research, than to a raw resource. But in addition to this standard criticism of increased exports of raw materials, there is also the fact that our exports of non-renewable raw materials can only be, by definition, finite.
Recent developments in the petroleum and natural gas situation make very clear the full force of this basic truth. Non-renewable resources are Canada's capital assets, and to continue to export them in a totally unrefined state is to sell off fixed assets to relieve a current expenses deficit. What this means is that the government should, above all else, be encouraging new industry and established industries in this country to grow and compete effectively at home and abroad. Unfortunately this budget before us illustrates the government's total lack of foresight and initiative in this area.
It is an economic fact of life that industrial and commercial expansion requires capital, Mr. Speaker. The Economic Council of Canada, in its 12th annual review, estimated that the nation's capital needs between now and 1985 will total between $800 and $860 billion dollars. By comparison, total investment expenditures over the past decade were around $200 billion. Thus a four-fold increase in capital outlays will be needed to increase productive facilities in line with the growth of Canadian markets, to develop and upgrade our energy and other natural resources, and to achieve the improvement in our productivity performance so urgently needed as a prerequisite for long-term price stability.
The pre-budget submission of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce states some of the needs of Canadian business quite succinctly:
Historically, 60-70 per cent of our investment has been financed by corporations through retained earnings and depreciation allowances.
Neither source is expected to advance in the future at the rates required. Depreciation allowances, based on original costs, are seriously inadequate to cover the replacement value of facilities. Profits, and hence retained earnings, are limited under the wage and price control program.
The submission continues:
It is therefore, in our opinion, imperative that the federal government continuously monitor the impact of the profit controls and provide, wherever possible, assistance to industry in the financing of productive capital investment.

June 8, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Portelance
Measures such as the deduction of inventory valuation adjustments from taxable income, or the provision of depreciation at the replacement value of assets, have been recommended before by the chamber . . . and are still needed.
In summary, the situation for industrial expansion in this country can be termed discouraging. At a time when the economic health of the country could be improved through such measures as research and development funding, tax reform for industry, lower personal income tax rates, and efforts to encourage public savings in order to increase available capital for investment in Canadian industry, the government has responded with a do nothing budget whose only significant message is that the government itself still refuses to curb its own expenditures.
The budget deficit will not recede. It will grow by about an estimated $5 billion in 1976-77. The increase in spending is 16.2 per cent, approximately what was projected in the estimates; the increase in revenues, 15.3 per cent.
As for the fiscal year just ended, the government has revealed that total government spending was $725 million higher than had been earlier forecast. That amounts to an increase of 18 per cent in government spending rather than the 16 per cent announced by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) when he unveiled some of the plans to restrain government spending last December.
I will conclude my comments, Mr. Speaker, by reiterating what this budget really means. It means that the government is content to go through the rest of this year with unemployment at about 7 per cent of the labour force, hoping that the 7.4 per cent unemployment rate recorded in April was just a fluke and not a real upturn. It calls for real growth of the economy of 5 per cent this year, and not much better next year. This very modest recovery depends, of course, on the economic stimulus offered by other countries, such as the United States, and not by any initiative of our own.
This budget calls for an inflation rate, as figured on the Gross National Product rather than consumer prices, of a hefty 9.5 per cent this year and about 6 per cent next year.
All in all, this non-budget presents us with a real example of what could only be expected from a government whose record of economic mismanagement is so considerable. Other countries have done and are doing better, and without the built-in advantages which make even bad management in Canada appear to be not so bad. Indeed what the Minister of Finance has provided us with is no budget at all. There can be no doubt that the government will have to show us a real budget in the near future.
Canadians have come to expect very little, except ineptitude, from the government, and so it is that we can only ask that a future budget demonstrate an understanding of the nation's problems, hope for the unemployed, and initiatives which will promote Canadian industry; but to ask this government for even a mediocre effort is to ask more than this government is capable of providing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Arthur Portelance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance

(Mr. Macdonald) for his budget. As many of my colleagues know, I have worked for a long time in the clothing industry, and I can therefore say that the minister provided us with a "made to order" suit but with very few alterations, which shows that we already had a good pattern. I also want to emphasize the enlightened determination shown in the proposed changes in our unemployment insurance legislation by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) who is also responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission and whom I have the pleasure to second as a parliamentary secretary. Incidentally, as you may guess, this will be the subject matter of my remarks today.
Everybody admits that the unemployment insurance formula had to be amended, but as in the fable of the miller, his son and the donkey, it was impossible to satisfy everybody at the same time. This debate has already shown that proposals range from the funnel to the Danaides' barrel. For instance, some members have blamed the minister for not going far enough in the area of restraints, especially among those who feel there are too many people who live poorly but pleasantly at the expense of what some people call the "permanently chronic workers" whereas on the other hand, it was said that this government was engaging in tax surgery at the expense of those who find it difficult to make both ends meet.
As a matter of fact, the changes before us had to be made, logically and in fairness, both for the large majority of Canadians who are working and paying for maintaining the present unemployment insurance system and for those who occasionally are the recipients of this system and who will finally benefit from it, for one has to keep in mind that the changes made to the Unemployment Insurance Act will bring about a substantial expansion of job creating programs. Our first goal, as the Minister of Manpower and Immigration said in his speech of June 2, is to provide jobs for as many Canadians as possible.
Unemployment insurance is not a goal but a step towards a new job. Those decisions are not made unexpectedly but are rather the result of analyses, surveys on conditions prevailing in Canada as well as other countries. Indeed I want to stress that even with the new clause extending from eight to twelve weeks the number of weeks of work necessary to become eligible for unemployment insurance, the Canadian formula is even more generous than in all industrialized nations of the world, except the Netherlands. In Sweden, you need 12 months of contribution, including five in the preceding year; in the United Kingdom, you need 26 weeks in the previous year to get the minimum benefits and 50 weeks for the maximum. In Germany, you need 26 weeks in the three preceding years. And when the NDP leader points out that in those countries unemployment rates are lower, I say to him that that is an argument which goes against his theory, since in all logic a lower rate of unemployment means that people find more jobs and also more quickly.
It would be useless to imagine, Mr. Speaker, that unemployment insurance alone can be used to right all our economic or social problems, even if it constitutes one of the most important and effective instruments available to the government to create jobs, as it is going to do more and
June 8, 1976

more with formulas of the local initiative type, and training programs are extremely important in that respect.
The minister has been criticized for not unwrapping immediately before the House all the programs in their finest details. Yet, those statements already contain the assurance that the amounts which will not be used for unemployment insurance will be spent to create jobs, with due consideration for regional needs. In the same line, the reform launched by the minister will allow us to calculate benefits according to the regional rather than the national rate of unemployment but all those amendments requiring the passage of legislation will only affect the true status of unemployment insurance recipients at the beginning of next year.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) already indicated that all plans for those enlarged manpower programs will be completed in two or three months and made public no later than this fall.
Canada is already regarded as leading the way in the creation of employment when, for instance, our Local Initiatives Program has been adopted in Great Britain while experts from the United States, France, Australia, etc, are considering it in their turn. The advantage of these programs is that they stimulate workers and respect the dignity of man, which, in many cases, helps bring back workers on the labour market. In my constituency of Gamelin, in Montreal, seven local initiatives projects made wonderful things this year not only for the hundred persons who took part in them, but for thousands of others who profited by them indirectly.
It is also certain that a pilot program launched in Newfoundland and which has known considerable success, will take great extension. Through that plan, hundreds of people have been able for about a year to continue to receive unemployment insurance benefits while attending training courses which enabled them to acquire qualifications they will be able to use on the labour market in sectors where they will be needed.
To continue on training, the minister reminded us in this House last week that with the addition of $40 million for industrial and institutional training, the federal government will have put $522 million in that sector alone during the present financial year. In the same way, the workers' mobility program has been made more generous.
Reverting to the subject of unemployment insurance, I must say that the next law will no longer include severance pay in the salary of an employee for purposes of establishing his unemployment insurance allowances. Similarly, the famous "four-week" rule will be eliminated thus enabling people without a job to take temporary employment and still be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. This could become an extremely efficient incentive.
The amendments suggested by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration do not only meet the wishes of politicians, journalists or social agencies. In the interesting declaration he made on June 2, the official critic of the Progressive Conservative Party for manpower, the hon. member for Hamilton-West (Mr. Alexander) said, I quote:
The Budget-Mr. Portelance
The Economic Council is of the opinion that our existing legislation induces people to join the unemployment rolls and is a disincentive to work. It estimates that present legislation induced between 70,000 and 80,000 people to go on unemployment.
I am sure that what the government wants, and what the whole House wants, is a formula which will help those who are in need, a formula which induces those who are unemployed to look for a job and to keep it. By the way, merging the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission will help to improve the situation in that particular area. Finally, Mr. Speaker, this formula is more practical, more efficient, more just and more realistically adapted to the needs of the Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, the journalists who are presently studying the situation are far from being unanimous. For example, last Thursday, the editorialist of the Globe and Mail estimated that the federal statistics on unemployment are no longer realistic because they consider as unemployed many people who do not really want to work or who do not want to get "bored" looking for a job. On the contrary, Charles Lynch, a journalist from the Southam News Agency, estimated that the progressive reduction, given the day before by the minister, in the number of those who claim unemployment insurance allowances among the so-called 8-to-ll week category and who would really have to face difficulties, was a calculation in which the statistics were sifted in a way very hard to control.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, no one of us can try the reins and the heart, as the saying goes. On the other hand, the demonstration of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration is based on the figures obtained from serious studies, and they prove, for instance, that the claimants of the "8 to 11 week" group cost 20 times, on the average, all the other recipients of unemployment insurance, that they use up their rights to the limit oftener, that they find work rather easily and quickly when they run out of unemployment benefits, that they often reenter the ranks of the recipients, that they are not usually the first breadwinner of the family but that their salary is added to the income of an average if not higher-income family, that they seldom if ever live on welfare, that their rate of claims is four times that of the average claim, in short that they are part of the category which is least exposed to having problems if an attempt is made to reduce the cost of unemployment insurance in a given sector.
Let us also remember that "disbursements" does not mean money taken from the worker, for it is understood that the amounts saved will be channelled towards programs for creating employment and training the workers, especially in those areas where the need is greatest. Finally, as the minister said again, the government does not seek the glory of reducing unemployment by one point or a fraction thereof, so much as, above all else, creating the largest possible number of jobs in the Canadian economy, as well as enabling the greatest possible number of Canadians to be advised of the existence of those jobs, to get them and keep them. That last point, namely that of keeping a job, illustrates well the importance of training programs which result in a more competent, better motivated and better remunerated labour force.
So we are not faced, as suggested by the New Democratic Party leader, with a sinister conspiracy to deprive those

June 8, 1976
The Budget-Mr. C.-A. Gauthier
unemployed who are most in need, and to let them treacherously on the street, but with the rational adjustment of the unemployment insurance system, so as to allow for instance more simple activities, the number of phases passing then from five to three, more generous operations because they will concurrently give way to some working forms or the registration for training courses, fairer activities because they will be more properly fashioned after regional requirements, finally more rational activities because they are based on the results of enquiries relating to the behaviour of certain categories of unemployment insurance recipients.
In the end, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that to get the maximum of success with the new regulations on unemployment insurance and employment creation programs, we surely need the cooperation of workers, but also that of employers, as well as of provinces with which the Minister of Manpower and Immigration indicated Wednesday his intention to attempt every collective effort. One should also note that several provinces as well have interesting programs to reduce the number of people on welfare from various categories, including-and I say this for our friends from the Social Credit Party-those in British Columbia. Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Manpower and Immigration said, these few legal and institutional changes will be introduced to promote a more efficient employment policy in this country, and I urge my colleagues to support the government position.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to congratulate the Minister of Finance for his courage in introducing this budget, because in the last number of years it has taken men of courage to prepare budgets.
In the way of summing up my thoughts on the subject, I endorse the following statement made by Claude Ryan in Le Devoir of May 27, and I quote:
Caught in the narrowest margin left a Canadian Minister of Finance for a long time, Mr. Macdonald introduced his first budget, in the House of Commons Tuesday evening, under very difficult circumstances which prompted many critics to suggest this may be his last budget.
Never in history did a federal budget come so close to being the "non-budget" it was immediately termed. Never in a long time did a Liberal Minister of Finance show so much reluctance and even shyness.
If I were to wish the minister something, it would be to hurry through that budget and avoid the path followed by his predecessors, who broke their necks at the head of that department we are tempted to call the death-trap ministry. As always, the budget tabled by the Minister of Finance for 1976-77 draws absolutely opposite reactions from businessmen and the millions of wage earners.
So it is not surprising that big corporations, banking monopolies and all the multinationals congratulate the Minister of Finance, while unionized and non-unionized workers alike and the 769,000 unemployed regret such an antisocial, not to say nationally shameful budget. But paradoxically, both sides may be right, since the government always favoured those who financed their elections, ignoring most of the time between elections those who were prevailed upon during the 60-day period to vote them back into power.

That is why I am wondering today which one is to blame-the governors or the governed who keep accepting to be easily taken in come every election time. It has been known by everybody, and this for 100 years, that successive governments have always protected the financial sector to the detriment of Canadians, and what is more astounding is that they have done so by making people believe that the elected government was acting in the best interests of Canadian workers.
The very proof of my allegations is found in the budget. After a somewhat in-depth review of the May 25, 1976 budget papers tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), one has only to look at page 11 of this paper and examine the list of anticipated expenses for 1976 to realize easily that 35 sectors will be favoured with an increase, whereas only four will suffer cutbacks, or sizeable reductions.
Even more astonishing is the fact that the very sectors which should have been increased, at least at the rate accepted by the Anti-Inflation Board, are those the government has decided to take a crack at-agriculture, unemployment insurance, Secretary of State and transport.
In my opinion the minister should have limited the CBC and CIDA budgets, the charges on the national debt as well as outlays for national defence, bank interests, government corporations and all the items under "other expenditures", which we had seven times without any explanation. We see that the budget of agriculture is reduced by $17 million whereas it should have been increased at least by $40 million to meet the demands of the industrial milk producers of Quebec which are more than reasonable; these producers are facing the worst problem ever experienced in this sector, due only to the decisions taken unilaterally by the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
Where is the logic of the government which after having eliminated 60 per cent of the small farms endangers 50 per cent of those which resisted the assault of the government? Having been invited and even encouraged to enlarge their farms, improve their buildings, modernize their techniques to obtain maximum efficiency, these producers are accused of overproduction only a few months later. Because the farm producers complied with the numerous requests of the Minister of Agriculture, because the industrial milk producers trusted the government's technocrats and technicians, the same producers are penalized for having listened to the government's specialists.
Has the Minister of Agriculture only thought about the financial effects on the milk producers? Is the government aware that instead of a 20 per cent decrease, those producers needed at least 15 per cent more than in 1975 to meet their financial obligations?
We must keep in mind that it is not of their own free will that the producers agreed to run into maximum debts to meet the department's requirements. The department should at least have the decency to recognize that it alone is responsible for the difficult financial situation of the industrial milk producers. Consequently, it is its responsibility, not anyone else's, not to request the producers to pay for its specialists' mistakes.
June 8, 1976

I can readily understand the march on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Thursday, June 3 to ask the Minister of Agriculture to reconsider his decision. Why Quebec more so than the other provinces? Because it is Quebec, more specifically the industrial milk producers in Quebec who are the most seriously affected. Indeed in the western provinces the production of industrial milk is insignificant. In Ontario, which produced its highest out of quota surpluses last year, the measure only normalizes the situation whereas the Quebec industrial milk producers who are responsible for only 2 per cent of all milk surpluses are those who must bear the burden of the cuts in quotas.
If the Minister of Agriculture really had to take drastic action to avoid more surpluses, why did he not emphasize restrictions for those who had a surplus last year? Why reduce regular quotas and why must those who did not fill their regular quotas last year be penalized,as well? That is where I see a lack of logic on the part of the department's experts, unless their deliberate purpose was to favour Ontario over Quebec. I believe the cause of all these problems is the total lack of long term dairy policy. Obviously it is much easier for the agriculture technicians to outline a 12 month policy than to make projections for five years ahead. Such a policy seems to be beyond the high officials of production and marketing of agricultural products. However, the possibilities are not lacking.
I am convinced it would cost less to the government to create a warehousing system for a five year period to restore balance between good and bad years. This would take us away from the vicious circle of surplus and shortage. Sometimes the federal government calls on producers, either in beef, pork, chicken, eggs or milk because a shortage is forecasted for a few months hence; the government makes promises to stimulate the production concerned. Producers go full steam ahead following the government incentives, only to learn 10 or 12 months later that they have caused a surplus. When shall we have enough competent people to stop playing this way with farm producers by making them support the burden of government mistakes or incompetence? Again, if producers were asked by the government to prepare farming policies we would have some reason to accuse and even punish these producers, but everyone knows full well that it is the officials who prepare and run all policies, whether they have to do with marketing or producing agricultural commodities. These officials are asked to think and to act for and on behalf of producers, but if officials make a mistake, the producers are quickly punished.
Further than that, today the Minister of Finance through his Anti-Inflation Board allows an increase of 12 or 15 per cent to all other groups of workers, indexed on the cost of living which is quite normal, but this same minister forces farmers and especially industrial milk producers to take a cut of 20 per cent in their income. Where is the consistency of the Ministers of Finance and Agriculture? I might add that it is discrimination against the Quebec dairy producers because, as I said earlier, once more Quebec bears the brunt. Indeed, when Canada had wheat surpluses, this same government compensated the western producers and even paid them not to sow wheat. Do I blame the western producers? On the contrary, I say to them: Good for you! I congratulate all hon. members from the west as I did then for imposing their will on the government and obtaining
The Budget-Mr. C.-A. Gauthier greater protection for farmers. Yet, the Liberals elected only a few members in the west, as is the case today; therefore it is not a partisan policy that prevailed but the pressure, the common sense policy.
If a handful of western members of the opposition have delivered that master stroke for their province, I wonder what the 59 elected Liberals in Quebec are doing. I fear that the Quebec Liberals are the victims of their strength in Parliament. Some surely have no backbone to uphold sincerely the interests of Quebec. Let us forget for a moment the condition of the party to think about Quebecers. The Quebec agriculture is ill and the cause is the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). Can my dear Liberal colleagues do something? It is up to them to show it in the days to come.
My second criticism is related to the $45 million which the minister wants to take away from unemployment insurance. I think that after agriculture, which will remain our basic industry for a few years, provided members remain conscious of their responsibilities in the House, a very important sector for the Quebec economy more particularly is the maintenance of the manpower and unemployment insurance services. Among the 750,000 unemployed in Canada, my region has a very high percentage and they are not wealthy unemployed, but people who are looking for a job and cannot find any. The minister knows quite well that when no more benefits will be paid to the unemployed, they will be compelled to register on the rolls on social welfare in Quebec.
That is a way as good as any other to shift his responsibilities on to the back of the provinces. That is a good example of the famous balance-sheet federalism of the present government. We forgot to tell one thing to the population: that federalism was profitable only to the central government. In 1942, after having made the provinces yield all their taxation rights, the central government went as far as promising to the naive provinces that it would reinstate them in their rights once the war would be over. Thirty-four years have passed since then and the federal government still retains most taxation rights. I would even say that it takes advantage of its taxation power to intrude every day into areas reserved exclusively to the provinces.
Just to give you an idea of it, during the study in a special committee before the presentation of the budget, I drew the attention of officials to the enormous difference between the increase in personal income tax and corporate income tax. In the document entitled "Budget Speech" of June 25, 1976, page 40, we can see that Canadian workers will pay $20 billion in direct taxes against $16 billion in 1975 which is an increase of more than $4 billion while big corporations will pay an additional $700 million only. This is another levy which demonstrates the absurdity of our taxation system. While we live in a period of great banking and financial monopolies, multinational companies which own 80 per cent of our economy pay only 24 per cent of the national budget, whereas salaried people pay 76 per cent of it.
We have been asking the government for years to restore the economic balance by getting the money from those who pocket revenues and file astronomical profits. Far from

June 8, 1976
The Budget-Mr. C.-A. Gauthier seeking to take the money where it really is so as to administer and guarantee each citizen an adequate minimum income to live on, the government turns back to the unemployed, to take more money from those who cannot even work to earn a decent living for themselves and their family.
As if he wanted to soften the blow, the minister first increased the premiums, and now he decides to reduce benefits. This is what I call administrative dishonesty. If the minister sincerely wants to save $75 or $100 million, he just has to turn to the Department of National Defence, and simply keep the $1 billion they intend to spend on the purchase of new toys for our soldiers overseas.
Let us talk a little bit, Mr. Speaker, of this famous Orion or Lockheed program, whichever one you wish to call it. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, that after we were told that the government could not afford to spend $40 million to help industrial milk producers, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) is prepared to run us into debt to the tune of $1 billion to buy new military planes. While everyone is clamoring for improved rail services, the Department of Transport budget is being reduced to fill in the coffers of national defence-I was about to say "international" since most of our forces are overseas.
The government proposes to close down railway lines which are unprofitable. But is the Air Force profit-making? The country cannot afford it, so what, there is no problem, Lockheed will finance the Orion deal. Do you not think there is something mysterious about the transactions of this corporation which inspired so much comments with the terrific bribes it has resorted to in several countries to boost its sales? After the Sky Shops scandal, shall we get another involving Lockheed?
When you listen to the sometimes quite harsh interventions in this House, you wonder if some ministers or civil servants have not succumbed to the temptation of bribes. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that it would have been better for the government itself to negotiate a little loan for the benefit of farmers. Bribes would have been less significant and it would have been compensated by a political gain.
I could not conclude without speaking of our great Crown corporation, Air Canada, and its unilingualism. I have no idea what the Prime Minister thinks of the disastrous events concerning his bilingualism program and what is going on at Air Canada. In light of those events we are more and more convinced that for some English-speaking Canadians bilingualism is a good and nice thing as long as it is not implemented. We are just seeing the beginning of a fight where many senior civil servants and some ministers will have to show their true face to the Canadian people. Even if you are part of Canada, when you dare prevent a province from using its own language it becomes dangerous, Mr. Speaker. As always, the minister promptly created a commission to hide behind but the problem is still there. And what a commission, Mr. Speaker! For a commission on bilingualism, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) could not do any better than chosing a lawyer who was a former adviser to the pilot association, a group absolutely hostile to bilingualism in Quebec's sky.
The Association des gens de l'air du Quebec denounced the appointment of Mr. Keenan and even declared that it would not cooperate in that inquiry because of the past

action of Mr. Keenan. The association went even further: it demanded the appointment of a French-speaking co-commissioner or Mr. Keenan's dismissal. The Minister of Transport said no to everything. It was the slap in the face given by our Minister of Transport to the airline employees in Quebec. However, witnessing the increasing rebellion in Quebec, Mr. Keenan realized that his appointment as commissioner had become litigious and, far from contributing to solve the problem, it was only increasing it, so he made a decision. We have seen that Mr. Keenan, in spite of his formal opposition to bilingualism, has more sense than the Minister of Transport. Now we are waiting for the creation of the new commission.
To my mind, the minister is too compromised at this point to designate alone the members of that commission. The cabinet must be very careful to avoid more confrontations. In the meantime, we Quebecers are paying our share of the deficits of the big beautiful unilingual company, Air Canada. If the minister wants to stay with the status quo at Air Canada, let him at least give money to the unemployed and the farmers in Quebec, the money we must pay for the deficits of Air Canada. Then only will we start to consider him as an impartial anglophone who tries to work for the unity of the two Canadian ethnic groups.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the debate on this budget of 1976, my mind went back over budget debates of the last 19 years. I think there is a well known expression, "The more things change, the more they remain the same".
We are suffering at this particular time from obvious evidence that the government did not know what to do and the civil servants did not know what to do, so they did nothing. I make that remark with some regret because I have seen one minister after the other in the last 25 years, going back to Walter Harris, suffer the same fate regardless of their politics because the elected representative was not contributing the knowledge that was available to the budget. We relied on the expertise of people who were sincere and able, but who had been consistently wrong for 30 years. I have made that remark on many a budget debate, and I regret to have to make it tonight. In a moment I shall refer to the source of this judgment. I always believe in being an optimist, however.
I was interested to read a statement by the former deputy minister of finance reported in the Globe and Mail of June 2. I shall not read the whole article but I would ask the members of the House who take seriously the part parliament should play in laying down the fiscal and monetary policy of this nation so as to maximize the good that will come from a proper policy, to pay particular attention to it. Here is a man who had been around for all of my time here and is now in private business. His concluding remark was: "Above all we economists should learn to be humble; so should our political leaders. Together we have much to be humble about." Now that Simon Reisman is free of government service he tells us to be humble because we have much to be humble about!
In my remarks tonight I am going to try to shift away from the details of this budget because there is general
June 8, 1976

agreement that it is a nothing budget. The minister himself made that very clear when he bragged that he would rather be cautious than foolhardy. I want to remind the House that along with a good many other people in Canada I have been seriously concerned this last year or so, as I saw the nation slowly begin to come out of the recession, that somebody would do something stupid to send us back into another recession.
In this history of mistakes over the last 30 years the situation we are in at this particular time in our economic cycle is exactly the same as on two other separate occasions in the years I have been in the House. On each of the previous occasions the circumstances were the same-a country slowly coming out of a recession and then the government did a stupid thing which sent the country into a worse recession.
Just before last Christmas I put the following question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) quietly at the end of the question period, as reported at page 10196 of Hansard:
. . . would the Prime Minister give serious consideration over the next three or four weeks to re-examining the whole course that the government is taking because I believe it is heading us toward a recession and would he turn the whole program of the government around into one of expansion so as to give the government time to get at the basic cause of inflation, which this program is not doing?
I was referring to the anti-inflation program. The Prime Minister promised he would give it serious consideration but as the House will understand, when he gave that answer he thought the expansion I asked about was the same type of expansion program we have had for 30 years from the advisers of the government. He thought it meant pumping more money into circulation so that there would be more to spend. He mentioned that in his answer. He said in effect, "Look how big our budgetary deficit is-we are expansionary." He accepted the word of the Department of Finance experts who believe that if we have a big budget deficit, that is expansionary. I say it is time the politicians took over from these experts and began to do some real thinking on the deficits that are before us.
Tonight I am not going to deal with the details of the budget. I am going to suggest that there are alternatives and these alternatives have been made public. They are not new but they are not being utilized by the advisers of our governments. I will give an example, Mr. Speaker.
First, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Water-loo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) for being the one speaker in the opening stages of this debate who looked at the situation in a philosophical sense and saw what the government was doing. All the government was doing was trying to take a political posture to get the Prime Minister out of the hole vis-a-vis those silly speeches he made around Christmas time.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge put forward not a new philosophy but one that was laid clear as an alternative by the Economic Council of Canada six or seven years ago, namely, that when you have a large number of unemployed and 15 per cent or 20 per cent of the plant capacity unused, if you put that group of people to work and put that plant capacity to use, then there is no inflation. Inflation only occurs when you try to put the people to work when there is not enough plant capacity. The name for this alternative is very well known; it is
The Budget-Hon. A. Hamilton called "potential budgeting". I hope it is the official policy of the New Democratic Party because when we form the government we can rely upon them as allies if they believe it. It is what we believe.
Everyone knows that if you use the labour force and use the plant capacity, the gross national revenue goes up, tax revenues go up, and the deficit comes down. This was used in the United States in 1964 when their budgeters reduced taxes by about $10 billion or $11 billion. Everyone said, "Disaster is upon us-here we have a big deficit and this crazy government comes along and reduces taxes by another $11 billion." But they put so many people to work and utilized so much plant capacity that when the year was over the government had $18 billion in new taxes and, instead of the familiar deficit, had a large surplus. This has only been used once in the United States to my knowledge, and it has never been used here. It is one alternative.
The second alternative is one I put forward some ten years ago in a series of three or four speeches. I suggested some refinements to the doctrine of Lord Keynes, and to keep it simple I called it "selective budgeting"-selective by region, selective by industry, and selective by social purpose. In those proposals I outlined how in a country as big as the United States or Canada the doctrines of Keynes would not work because they were designed for a small country like the United Kingdom. In Canada there are many regions and a great variety of sophistication in industries and great differences in social need. Any Canadian budget of the future should contain this selective feature.
I know these ideas were heeded because there is occasional evidence in a budget that they are known. In the last budget there was a reasonable concession to the mari-times on unemployment insurance. I would suggest that the principle of selective budgeting should be applied systematically in all phases of economic activity if we are to make this large country, with 16 or 18 different regions, work.
Those are two alternatives, Mr. Speaker. I shall now put forward a third alternative that to my knowledge has not been publicly formulated anywhere in Canada. The person who enunciated this doctrine is a Canadian, for which I give him full credit. His name is Mundell. For years he lectured at Waterloo. His quantitative analysis of those ideas followed over the years by our economic masters proved that those so-called truths are not truths at all; exactly the opposite is the case. Although this evidence has been accumulating for almost 15 years, it has not come to the attention of ministers of the Crown or ministerial advisers. Actually, there is a complete black-out of knowledge. There is no talk of the Mundell hypothesis.
Professor Laffer of the University of Chicago has also done quantitative analysis work confirming the correctness of the Mundell hypothesis. The hypothesis can now be described as the Mundell-Laffer hypothesis. In a nutshell, it says that assumptions which economists of all western nations have held to be truths are not truths at all. For instance, economists have assumed that when a country experiences a negative balance of trade in intangibles and tangibles, you should reduce the value of your currency.

June 8, 1976
The Budget-Hon. A. Hamilton Theoretically that move should automatically eliminate your international trade deficit. Actually it will not eliminate the deficit but increase inflation in direct proportion to the amount of devaluation.
Professor Laffer demonstrated with figures based on quantitative studies that our government advisers and the advisers to governments in most countries of western Europe have been following false doctrine. Conventional economists hold that if you have a deficit balance of trade you should automatically devaluate your currency. Yet West Germany, Taiwan, and Brazil have been doing very well by not following that doctrine.
I will not deal at length with the international ramifications of the Mundell-Laffer hypothesis. The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) will speak in this debate tomorrow. He is much more capable than I am of explaining the mysteries of economic workings. I want to relate that particular hypothesis to the domestic stance our government ought to take at this time, to show that nearly everything we have done in the fiscal field for 30 years has been wrong.
By the way, for those hon. members interested in serious reading I recommend a royal commission report which came out in 1964. It traces the economic history of Department of Finance policies for 30 years. One truth emerges from the report, and it is this. All our advisers to the government have been constant in one thing: they have been constantly wrong, both in advising as to the direction the government should take and in timing. Read chapter 20. Hon. members will see that not only the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain talks this way. The royal commission report has been available for 12 years, but there is no evidence to show that elected representatives of the people have even read it. It would give them ammunition with which to challenge their advisers whose advice has resulted in the type of crap we have had in the last several budgets.
What would Mundell do in present day circumstances? Since our economic charts are slowly levelling off instead of rising, and since there is unused plant capacity and slack in the labour force, Mundell would advise a policy of fiscal ease. Some would call that a policy of budgetary expansion. But the expansion should not be brought about by increasing the deficit, not brought about simply by cutting taxes across the board to encourage people to spend more and spend their way out of recession. That is not what he means. Neither is he thinking of handouts or transfer payments. He suggests that in times like these we should make full use of our labour force and plant capacity. We should achieve our purposes by instituting tax cuts which will affect regions and industries. In that way we could fulfil our social purposes. For example, our steel industry for the next 30 years will have tremendous opportunity. Let us back the industry and encourage it to take advantage of its opportunity.
Our steel production figures should be rising steadily; instead, in 1976 we have witnessed a decline in steel production. Canada among the western nations can boldly compete with anyone in steel. We pay higher wages per hour, produce better steel, and do it more cheaply than our competitors. Why should we not back our steel industry

and encourage it to expand in the west and in the mari times?
I would not oppose something several speakers have mentioned in this debate, imaginative tax incentives to encourage export efforts. You will notice that I did not use the word "goods." In the next 25 or 30 years a great proportion of Canadian exports will not consist of goods.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, they will be raw materials.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Our
exports will consist of the know-how of our people, of our engineers, miners, and scientists. Their expertise is needed in the Middle East, Africa, the Far East, and even in countries more sophisticated in certain respects than we are, for we are expert in certain fields. Mr. Speaker, in certain fields of knowledge we have developed expertise which is beyond price. Price is not the criterion. I should like to see tax reductions to encourage such export efforts. That is one alternative under the fiscal ease policy of the Mundell hypothesis.
The second point concerns capital accumulation. Members on both sides of the House have spoken of this many times in the last three or four years. When I talk of capital accumulation I talk of many facets of saving. First, we must consider straight savings. The high interest rates of today are not only killing industry and governments; they are killing people trying to build a home, start a business, or buy a farm. If you take a $50,000 mortgage for 30 years at 12 per cent, you will pay $150,000 in interest charges on top of the principal sum of $50,000. Seventy-five per cent of the cost of buying a home, starting a mine or opening a business, consists of interest charges. High interest rates are the common enemy of the government, the business world, and the consumer. I say that capital accumulation in any form is good.
I notice that there was faint praise for the minister because he increased the exemption under registered retirement savings plans to $5,500. I will not give him faint praise. I say it was a good thing to do. I hope my NDP friends remember that we have a labour force of between eight million and nine million people; half the homes of that labour force are paid for. Their kids are educated. They want to take advantage of a registered retirement savings plan, to add to their pension on top of their company's pension. When you look at the figures it becomes apparent that more than a few people are using these plans. I suggest that around four million Canadians are taking advantage of them. Pretty soon I hope six million or eight million will take advantage of them. I say to the minister, good for him. It is good to invest the money that way. Unfortunately some pension plans put money to nonproductive uses.
Then we must consider the question of equity. Equity is the key whereby Canadians as individuals will own their own country. They will not own their own country if the state takes everything over; they can only own it as individuals. This means that we must put money into equity in such a way that Canadians not only own the majority of our resource and manufacturing industries, but control them. I have spoken on this before, and I must put it very bluntly, Mr. Speaker. Unless Canadians as individuals take over the ownership of these companies,
June 8, 1976

then what is happening so rapidly today will soon be over. Every time there is a problem, all the provincial government and federal government advisers can say is socialize them. If we continue taking over industry at the rate we are moving today in the so-called enterprise parties, by the year 1990 all the money earned by Canadians will come from government owned institutions.
There are some who would advocate that, but certainly not the NDP because they could not get any members elected if they did. It is coming from our civil servants who believe that the individual businessman, farmer, or labour union is not competent to make his or their own decisions. Therefore this question of accumulating capital through equity is the key.
The second type of savings is the more rapid circulation of money. I congratulate the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan), who was here a moment ago, for accepting the proposal I made to him some time ago, in that in so far as northern oil and gas is concerned we are taking off front end loading charges and not taxing them until they get their debt paid off. Then we will take a much larger percentage than we would have got before. I say congratulations are due to that minister for accepting that principle and listening to ideas from this side.
I ask the government and the people of Canada to realize that if you are going to get these huge interest payments down, you have to speed up the flow of capital. If you can pay off a debt in four years instead of 12 years, that is the same as having three times as much money. If there is three times as much money in Canada, interest rates have to come down. The Keynesians say that if we print more money, interest rates will have to come down. This has been proved wrong for 30 years.
We have to increase the amount of capital, with hopefully more and more going into equity. However, before you can ask someone to go into equity you have to get governments off his back in order to allow him to earn some dividends on his equity. Then he has something at the end of his life instead of it all being taken away by inflation and taxation.
More rapid circulation could be applied, not just to northern gas, but to all capital intensive enterprises. In that I include homes for our people. I gave the example of taking 30 years to pay off a $50,000 mortgage. Cut that time to ten years and you cut the interest rate from $150,000 to $27,000. There is a $123,000 saving by the fast payout. Give the money to somebody else and get the interest rates down.
I sit here and writhe as I see young people taking on horrendous mortages, knowing they will be in debt until they are old men and women, when there is a way to get away from it. The answer, as Mundell points out, is to get back to some old fashioned economics; when interest rates are high pay the debts off quickly. That is simple.
The third point I want to bring up under the Mundell-Laffer hypothesis is labour management. I am glad to see the former Minister of Labour, now Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), in the House. He knows the truth of what I am going to say. One of the people to get all the blame for
The Budget-Hon. A. Hamilton high costs is labour. In trying to protect themselves from high interest costs, land costs, and government costs, they grab for more and more in order to stay in the race. This becomes part of the cost-push and they get all the blame for it.
The minister knows there is a better way of doing these things. We have an example, not of the controls the government is using, but of a story that was leaked about a month ago, May 4. A union which had been constantly fighting management, and management constantly fighting the union, came to light in a report in the Globe and Mail of May 4. It actually appeared in the Vancouver Sun the day before. I quote:
Canada's West Coast grain handling industry and the grain handlers union have taken a far-reaching and unprecedented step by agreeing to submit their differences over wages in a new agreement to arbitration.
One of the union men said:
-the move to arbitration was taken because the union in no circumstances could be a party to halting the flow of grain through West Coast ports.
It would have been disastrous for all concerned.
It would have been disastrous for management, union men, the consumer, and the farmer. Editorials came out stating how wonderful it was that some guys had agreed to something. The minister knows what I am getting at. I say that when the full story is told, it will be found that that story started here in the House of Commons and the minister is present who asked me the question. A group of members of parliament went out and took a little part in that. God bless them, they kept quiet this past year and a half and let the deal jell. Now we have the union and management agreeing.
Strikes are not necessary. We all lose with strikes. Mutual advantage says we should get rid of them. Indeed when the full story is told we can take this precedent and move it into many other sections of industry where we can measure quantitatively the amount of production, find out what the men want, and what management wants. We can get them both on the road and stop these absurd strikes without any law at all. All that is necessary is mutual observation and advantage. My time is running out, but I wish to ask this question. What was there in this budget to encourage labour and management to put an end to the obsolete confrontations that have developed over the past 30 years?
I will not say anything more about the cost of government or urban land costs. I have spoken on those subjects before. I want to conclude by simply saying that in this budget-tackling a few things, not causing any waves- there was no attempt whatever to use the time that the price and wage controls give to government to get at the six structural causes of inflation.
The government is betraying the people of Canada by forcing these controls. It is taking away the right of men and management to meet and deal as equals. It is not using the time on things which are well known. This is nothing more than a straight John Turner budget. It is nothing but civil service gobbledygook, trying to prove theories that were proven wrong 30 years ago. This budget cannot be supported by people who believe in growth, and the Conservative party went on record today, in the words of its

June 8, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Caccia
leader, as the party of growth in Canada, and there we stand.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about 12 days ago, on the first day of this debate, the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) made a very accurate observation. He stated that the greatest contradiction of the Conservative position on this budget was the suggestion that the government could at one and the same time cut spending, cut taxes, and cut its deficit, while stimulating faster growth and employment. When asked to explain how to accomplish this feat, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) replied that it was because the private sector was going to be given a chance. Not even the Canadian Chamber of Commerce would subscribe to such nonsense.
In its pre-budget brief to the government the Canadian Chamber of Commerce stated that if it was considered necessary to inject some stimulus into the economy in order to alleviate high unemployment, there should be a tax reduction to provide an investment incentive. However, the chamber clearly recognized that such a cut would reduce government revenues and add to the prospective cash deficit for the current year. The chamber maintained that the proposal should not exceed that which they forecast for last year of $5.5 billion. The actual cash requirement was almost $1 billion below that of last year, and the government expects it will be about the same level this year, which is well below the maximum prescribed by the Chamber of Commerce.
In his speech the hon. member for York-Simcoe alleged that the accumulated deficits of the government would come to about $11.5 billion-presumably, from the context of his remarks, he came to that conclusion on a national accounts basis-by the end of this year. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the net deficit from 1968-69 to that projected for the current fiscal year amounts to $7.7 billion, which means a difference, a discrepancy, an error, of nearly $4 billion on the part of the financial critic of the Conservative party.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what kind of a leader, and what kind of a position in the country can that party expect to have in the eyes of Canadians when their financial critic makes a mistake of $4 billion in a major speech in this debate? If I can express a hope, Mr. Speaker, give us back any time the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies); we would welcome him back. The greatest sin that he committed was that of contradicting himself once every six months, but he certainly never made mistakes of this magnitude.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe complained that since 1968 direct personal taxes, as a share of total federal revenue, had increased from 34 per cent to around 53 per cent, whereas the share of corporate tax revenue had remained constant at 15 per cent. It should be pointed out here that the hon. member's figures are once again in error. He has compared the revenues from personal tax in 1968 on a budgetary basis with those projected for the current year on a national accounts basis, which of course, Mr. Speaker, is like comparing apples and oranges, something that the hon. member for York-Simcoe frequently does.

On a national accounts basis, personal direct taxes accounted for about 40 per cent of total federal revenues in 1968, not 34 per cent. They are forecast to represent around 53 per cent of total revenues in the current fiscal year.
While the hon. member for York-Simcoe condemns the increase in federal spending in recent years and the size of federal deficits, he conveniently ignores the fact that rarely a day goes by in this House of Commons when a member of the Conservative party does not press either for increased expenditure for this or that purpose-sometimes expenditures involving tens of millions of dollars-or opposes increased charges for public services or reduced subsidies aimed at reducing the deficit of the treasury.
This great financial critic of the Conservative party ignores an even more fundamental fact, that the admittedly large increase in government spending of the last few years has primarly been due to these two factors: first, the impact of inflation on the government's own cost of providing goods and services; secondly, increases in government expenditures undertaken to ease the adverse impact on the Canadian people of inflation and recession.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe accused the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) of "fiddling" and "diddling" and cooking the books-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the best line you have had all evening.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-misrepresenting charges, and so on. He complained that the main estimates tabled earlier this year projected expenditures by the Post Office of $981 million in 1975-76, whereas the budget papers tabled by the finance minister showed expenditures for last year of only $901 million. Since the increase in Post Office expenditures projected in the estimates for the current year would be significantly more when compared to actual expenditures last year, as opposed to the projection contained in the main estimates, the member proposed to lop $95 million off the total for the current year. However, the member failed to take account of a very simple fact, namely, the prolonged strike of postal workers last year which resulted in expenditures being significantly less than provided for in the estimates. Surely not even the hon. member for York-Simcoe would advocate a repeat of this kind of enforced cost control.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe contends that because of other similar differences between spending projections in the main estimates prepared last December and preliminary actual spending projections contained in the budget papers, there was room for a saving totalling $225 million. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is, of course, the most specious kind of argument.
The hon. member maintains that some $410 million can be saved from the non-budgetary side of the accounts, but does not tell us where he proposes to make cutbacks. He proposes to slash spending under the heading of "professional and special services" by $250 million. Coming from a Conservative, this is the greatest proposal for spending reductions! He apparently chooses to remain oblivious to the fact that expenditures under this category are for
June 8, 1976

services and facilities which are acquired from outside the federal government, because they can be obtained at considerably less cost than if we tried to provide them through government agencies.
Nearly 40 per cent of the total, for example, goes to purchase educational and manpower training services from the provinces. Large outlays are also incurred to purchase outside computer services, private security services, medical services, and to obtain legal and architectural services which in many instances can be provided far more efficiently by the private sector than by the government itself. Yet we have the hon. member for York-Simcoe, that great financial critic, expounding a theory which is diametrically opposed to that of his party.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the member proposes to save $140 million through administrative savings and amalgamating existing departments, or phasing out federal operations which overlap provincial operations. The hon. member proposed to make about $140 million disappear, but he was reluctant to tell us how he would do it. There is, however, a particular obligation upon this great financial critic-and as I say, give us back the hon. member for Don Valley any time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is an obligation on him in view of the fact that at their last policy convention the Tories approved several measures which would have the effect of significantly increasing the number of federal departments and agencies. When examined in detail in quickly becomes apparent that the "savings" of more than $1 billion conjured up by the hon. member for York-Simcoe are nothing more than the stuff that dreams are made of.
The amendment before us speaks of the failure on the part of the government to realize job creation. I should like to put on the record for the benefit of hon. members, in case their memories are short, the record of job creation on the part of the Liberal government. If we look at the job creation statistics that have been provided by OECD-and no one can claim that OECD statistics are partisan so far as Canadian politics are concerned-we find 472,000 jobs approximately were created between 1970 and 1972, 394,000 in 1972-73, 393,000 in 1973-74, and between 1974 and the last quarter of 1975, 552,000 new jobs, for a total of 1,811,000 new jobs created, and this is in a country with a population of only 22 million people. I would ask, Mr. Speaker, is that not a fantastic performance in job creation in this country?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: Let us consider for a moment this lack of confidence on the part of the Tories in this great nation of ours. Does this mean there is a lack of confidence in Canada when we have foreign investment pouring in every year?

If anyone has a lack of confidence in Canada it is the Conservative party. That is what their amendment is all about. The amendment speaks about the lack of long-term growth and job potential and economic growth. It speaks of the lack of ability to create jobs.
This afternoon we heard from the new leader of the Conservative party. I could not help but think of the good old times when the leader of the Conservative party was the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), and I think of that party's lack of confidence in that leader. That was really shocking to the whole country when they dumped their leader.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: It was your decision, and it is up to you to draw your own conclusions. Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the government for its ability in steering a fine course at a very difficult financial moment.
